blocks.text: The basic mechanism of replication is similar in all organisms. The steps below are for prokaryotes; eukaryotes use almost the same mechanism.

items: Replication begins at a specific sequence called the replication origin site: one in prokaryotes, many along the DNA in eukaryotes. An initiator protein binds there and starts the process.
Helicases ('unwinding' enzymes) break the hydrogen bonds between base pairs; the strands separate a little into two Y-shaped replication forks, together a replication bubble.
Unwinding produces supercoils ahead of the fork; the enzyme gyrase (a topoisomerase) attaches ahead of the fork and relieves them.
Single-strand binding proteins hold the single strands apart and stop them re-joining. The two forks move away from each other, and both strands act as templates.

blocks.text: New DNA cannot start on a bare template. The enzyme primase lays down a short stretch of 5-10 RNA nucleotides, the primer, on each template at the origin.

blocks.alt: A replication bubble: the double helix opens in the middle and a replication fork lies at each end. At each fork gyrase sits on the duplex ahead and helicase at the fork; yellow single-strand binding proteins hold the separated strands apart; a purple primase lays a short primer on a template strand near each fork. The duplex ends are marked 5' and 3'.

blocks.text: DNA polymerase III, the main builder among polymerases I, II and III of prokaryotes, takes free nucleotides and matches them to the exposed template, A with T and C with G. The raw materials are deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP); as each is attached two phosphates are broken off, releasing energy for the building.

Polymerase III can add a nucleotide only to the 3' end of an existing one, so it extends the primer and keeps adding in the 5' to 3' direction. The two template strands run in opposite directions, so they are copied differently. On the template running towards the fork, the enzyme moves the way the DNA unzips and builds the leading strand continuously. On the other template it must move away from the fork; as the DNA opens it jumps back to a new primer, building short Okazaki fragments, so this lagging strand is made in stops and starts.

blocks.title: For information and tidbits
blocks.text: DNA polymerase I supports polymerase III by replacing the primers; polymerase II repairs DNA damage during the cell's life. An RNA primer marks the error-prone starting stretch as temporary, making it easy to remove later. The leading strand can grow from one primer, but the lagging strand needs a new primer for each Okazaki fragment, named after the Japanese scientist who discovered them.

Replication ends at a specific termination site; the DNA between an origin and a termination site is a replication unit, or replicon. DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primers and fills the gaps with DNA nucleotides, including gaps between Okazaki fragments, and DNA ligase joins the fragments of the lagging strand. Each new DNA keeps one original strand and one new strand, so half of the original molecule is conserved in each generation.

blocks.alt: One replication fork. Ahead of it gyrase sits on the parental double helix and helicase opens the strands. On the upper arm DNA polymerase III makes the leading strand continuously towards the fork. On the lower arm the lagging strand is made away from the fork as Okazaki fragments, each starting with an RNA primer made by primase; DNA polymerase III extends each fragment, DNA ligase joins them and single-strand binding proteins hold the template open.

blocks.title: For information: replication in biotechnology
blocks.text: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) copies a specific DNA billions of times; recombinant DNA technology cuts DNA from different sources and amplifies it by replication; genome sequencing makes many copies of a genome to read its sequence; and diagnostic tests copy sections of a patient's DNA to look for mutations that indicate a genetic disorder.

Stability means DNA is copied accurately: DNA polymerase III and the eukaryotic polymerases proofread to keep the nucleotide sequence, which maintains an organism's traits and keeps its cells working. Variability is the exception: occasionally a permanent change, a mutation, occurs, from errors in replication or from environmental factors. Variability is the main source of new traits, lets populations adapt to changing environments and is the raw material of evolution.
